query: W melts near 3422 °C, whereas Cu boils near 2562 °C, so conventional induction or arc-plasma casting cannot readily yield a uniform W–Cu material. Phase separation and void formation can impair thermal transport. Filling a W skeleton with molten Cu or Cu powder can leave defects; spark-plasma sintering and mechanical alloying can produce finer, more uniform structures but can also leave voids; vapor-coated W powders have been sintered to achieve near-perfect contact between the constituents; and metal 3D printing has also been explored. Starting from W particles or connected W regions within a Cu matrix for heat transfer under irradiation in fusion-reactor joints, what single intervention could overcome these limitations while preserving mechanical durability? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts an outcome relative to a named existing fabrication baseline, defines the processing and service boundaries, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment and observations that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: An ultrathin ALD-deposited interlayer on tungsten (W) particles will improve the wettability of molten copper (Cu) during spark-plasma sintering, reducing void formation and phase separation and thereby enhancing both thermal transport and mechanical durability relative to conventionally processed W–Cu composites.
generation.material_initial_state: Tungsten particles dispersed within a copper matrix processed through conventional routes (e.g., spark-plasma sintering or mechanical alloying) that typically exhibit interfacial voids and phase separation defects.
generation.intervention: Apply an ultrathin wetting interlayer on W particles using atomic layer deposition (ALD) prior to sintering.
generation.conditions: Sintering under a controlled vacuum and at optimized sub-solidus temperatures that promote rapid, uniform interfacial diffusion without reaching melting or boiling temperatures, thereby preventing high thermal gradients.
generation.structural_mediator: An ALD-originated ultrathin coating that forms a chemically compatible interface between W and Cu, enabling improved wetting and minimized void formation.
generation.mechanism: The ALD coating reduces interfacial energy barriers, thereby enhancing Cu wettability on W. This facilitates uniform interfacial diffusion during sintering, which reduces the likelihood of defect formation (voids and phase separation) and leads to a denser, mechanically robust composite with enhanced thermal conductivity.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline uncoated composites, the ALD-treated composites will display a lower void fraction, improved interfacial contact, enhanced thermal conductivity, and maintained or improved mechanical durability under high-temperature conditions typical of fusion-reactor joints.
generation.baseline: W–Cu composites produced by conventional methods such as spark-plasma sintering and mechanical alloying without any ALD surface modification.
generation.boundary: The processing window is limited to sub-solidus sintering conditions under vacuum and the material is intended for high-temperature service in heat transfer applications, specifically fusion-reactor joint environments.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative improvement in thermal conductivity and void reduction remains uncertain without experimental validation, and the optimal ALD interlayer material and thickness require further optimization.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of W–Cu composites using identical spark-plasma sintering conditions: one set using ALD-coated W particles and one set using uncoated W particles. Characterize the interfacial microstructure, void content, thermal conductivity, and mechanical properties.
measurements: Void fraction via scanning electron microscopy (SEM) or x-ray computed tomography
Interfacial bonding quality using transmission electron microscopy (TEM)
Thermal conductivity using laser flash analysis
Mechanical durability via compressive strength and fatigue testing
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the ALD-coated composites do not show statistically significant improvements in reduced void fraction, enhanced interfacial bonding, increased thermal conductivity, and improved mechanical durability compared to the uncoated baseline, the hypothesis would be falsified.

chosen.technique: atomic layer deposition (ALD) to deposit an ultrathin wetting layer on W particles
chosen.conditions: Sintering under controlled vacuum and temperature conditions that promote rapid, uniform interfacial diffusion while avoiding phase separation and excessive void formation
chosen.why: The phase separation and void formation problem (niche 2) is central to impairing thermal transport. By employing ALD to coat tungsten particles with an ultrathin interlayer, the wettability of Cu is improved during sintering, ensuring near-perfect contact without compromising mechanical durability. ALD is a well-established, scalable technique that provides atomic-scale control over interface composition and thickness, directly addressing the limitations of previous methods and thereby offering a clear, controlled experiment to falsify the hypothesis if voids and phase separation persist.
